results.author: Becky from Ohio
results.title: Rockefeller Center at Christmas — absolutely unreal!
results.content:
Okay so I just got back from my first ever trip to NYC and I HAVE to tell you all about Rockefeller Center because WOW. I've seen it in movies a million times (like Home Alone 2 obviously and also Elf which is basically a documentary about NYC right??) but nothing prepares you for seeing it in person. The Christmas tree is just massive. Like I knew it was big but I didn't KNOW it was THAT big. And the ice skaters below — I could have watched them for hours. The whole complex has this energy that's electric especially around the holidays.

We did Top of the Rock (get the CityPASS, it saves a bunch) and the view is insane. You can see the Empire State Building, Central Park, the whole Hudson River. I just stood there with my mouth open for like ten minutes. The elevator ride up is cool too — the ceiling lights up with an animation which was a fun touch.

The concourse underneath has shops and food — we grabbed pizza and wandered for another hour. Best part is you don't need a ticket for any of that. The whole lower level and outdoor plaza are totally free to walk through, so if you're on a budget you can still soak up the atmosphere. The Art Deco details are gorgeous — gold accents and geometric patterns everywhere. My phone gallery is basically 80% Rockefeller Center photos now.

Huge tip — go on a weekday! We went Thursday and while it was busy it wasn't insane. Weekend holiday crowds are total chaos apparently. The staff are super helpful if you need directions because the complex is huge and I got turned around at least three times trying to find the right elevator. But even getting lost is fun — you discover random cool art installations.

I cannot recommend this enough. If you're going to NYC for the first time, this has to be on your list. It's touristy but things are touristy for a reason right?

results.author: BiteSizedReviews
results.title: Peter Luger Steak House: A 135-Year-Old Porterhouse Worth Every Dollar
results.content:
I finally made it to Peter Luger Steak House last week, and I've got thoughts. Let me start with the booking situation — you absolutely need a reservation here. Like, weeks in advance for a weekend slot. I booked about three weeks out and the earliest I could get was a 5:45 PM Tuesday. So plan accordingly.

The restaurant sits on Broadway in Williamsburg, in this heavy, dark, wood-paneled building that looks exactly like what you'd imagine a 135-year-old steakhouse would look like. Inside it's all dark oak, stained glass, and white-jacketed waiters who seem to have been working there since the 1970s. The service is brusque but I'd say efficient rather than rude — these guys know their job and they do it fast.

On to the food. The famous bacon appetizer — a thick-cut slab of smoked, sugar-cured bacon — is probably the best single bite on the menu. It's $18 and absolutely worth it. The star of the show is the porterhouse for two, at about $120. They bring it out on a sizzling pewter platter, already sliced, swimming in butter and juices. The crust is exceptional — a deep, dark char from the broiler. The meat itself is USDA Prime, dry-aged for about four weeks. It had that distinctive nutty, funky dry-aged flavour that you either love or find overwhelming. I personally lean towards loving it. The interior was a perfect medium-rare, though I will say the slices closest to the bone end ran closer to medium-well, which is worth noting.

Sides are good but not revelatory. The German fried potatoes are crispy and oniony — solid. Creamed spinach is rich and garlicky. The steak sauce (their house-made Luger sauce) is tangy and horseradish-forward. I'd skip it if your steak is cooked well, though.

Cash only, which everybody warns you about. They have an ATM in the basement. I found parking about a block away on a weekday evening — street parking exists but you'll circle a few times.

Pricing: about $100 per person including the bacon, a steak for two, two sides, and tip. That's actually reasonable for this quality in NYC, in my opinion. The service charge is set at 20% on parties of six or more but standard tipping otherwise.

Overall? It's the definitive New York steakhouse experience. Is it the best steak in the city? Probably not — places like Keens and Minetta Tavern give it serious competition. But the whole package — the history, the atmosphere, the ritual of it — that's what you're really paying for.

results.author: Julia Chen
results.title: Taking Kids to The Met: A Survival Guide for Parents
results.content:
If you're thinking about taking your kids to The Metropolitan Museum of Art, here's what I wish someone had told me before our first trip. We've now taken our two boys (ages 6 and 9) three times, and I've learned the hard way what works.

First thing: book your timed tickets online. I cannot stress this enough. The museum requires reservations now even for general admission, and if you show up without one on a weekend you might be waiting an hour or turned away entirely. We booked the first slot at 10am and got straight in.

Second: go straight to the information desk and ask for the family guide and the scavenger hunt cards. Both are free and they saved our entire visit. The scavenger hunt has the kids looking for specific artworks — a monkey, a suit of armor, a boat — and it kept my 6-year-old engaged for a solid two hours. The family guide has route suggestions broken down by age group.

Third: the 81st Street entrance is your friend. If you're pushing a stroller, skip the main Fifth Avenue steps and enter through the ground-level entrance on 81st Street. It's flat ground with no stairs and you go straight into the Egyptian wing which is the most kid-friendly area anyway. The whole museum is great with strollers thanks to elevators between floors.

Fourth: budget for a meal because you won't make it through a full day without eating. The cafeteria on the ground floor is loud and kid-tolerant, with pizza, pasta, and chicken fingers that my boys actually ate. Not gourmet but fine for what it is. Pack snacks in your bag too — the cafe can get expensive for a family of four.

The arms and armor gallery is the number one kid magnet. My boys spent forty minutes just staring at the knights on horseback. The Egyptian wing with the mummies is a close second. Skip the European paintings unless your kids are unusually patient — the art is amazing but three-year-olds don't care about Rembrandt.

Bathroom access is good. There are clean restrooms on every floor with changing tables. No serious complaints there.

We stayed about three hours which was enough. By the end everyone was tired and the gift shop almost bankrupted me. If you're visiting New York with kids I'd honestly say this is a must-do — just go in with a plan and lower your expectations about how much culture you'll actually absorb.

results.author: jenny_torres
results.title: Brooklyn Bridge Park — Why I Still Come Back After Ten Years
results.content:
I remember when Pier 1 was just concrete slabs and chain-link fence. Back in 2015, right after they opened that first section, I'd sneak down there with a coffee before work and sit on a bench watching the sun hit the Watchtower building. Nobody else around — just seagulls and the occasional jogger. Now? The lawn's packed every warm weekend, you can barely find a square of grass. And honestly? Good for them. I mean it. The park used to be this weird secret us Brooklyn Heights people kept to ourselves, and now it's everyone's, and it should be.

I live on Montague Street, so the park's basically my backyard. My dog Mochi knows the walk to Pier 6 by heart — she starts pulling at the leash when we hit Columbia Heights. They've got water stations for dogs near the playground, which is a lifesaver in August. I've watched that Pier 6 playground grow from a bare sandpit to this elaborate wooden castle structure my niece calls 'the pirate ship.' Last time she visited we spent three hours there and she still cried when we left.

What gets me is how different each pier feels. Pier 2 is chaos — basketball courts, roller skaters, music blasting. Pier 3 is the weird quiet one where the ecology nerds go — saw a heron there last month, just standing in the marsh like it owned the place. Pier 5 is soccer families and cricket on Sundays. It's the same riverfront but every pier has its own personality. I love that.

The skyline thing though — I never get tired of it. Even after a decade, I'll be walking Mochi at dusk and catch the Empire State Building lit up across the water and think yeah, okay, I live here. That's still pretty good.

Oh, and one thing that's changed: the food trucks are way better now. The old hot dog cart on Furman got replaced by Arepa Lady's cousin or something — best cachapas I've had outside Queens. But that's not what I come for. I come for the quiet mornings before the crowds show up, when it's still mine for a little while.

results.author: britt_from_boston
results.title: First timer at Katz's — what to order??
results.content:
britt_from_boston: Okay so I'm finally going to Katz's for the first time next weekend and I'm SO excited. I've seen it in a million movies and I know I HAVE to get the pastrami but is that enough? Do I need a side? What about the soup? Also how does the ticket system work because I'm terrified I'll lose it and have to pay fifty bucks. And is it crazy busy on a Saturday around 2pm? Can I take photos at the famous booth? Sorry I just really don't want to mess this up!

deli_king_nyc: Okay so first — pastrami on rye is the move. Get it with mustard. Matzo ball soup is killer but the sandwich is massive so maybe share it. Get the hand-cut fries and a half-sour pickle. Ticket system is simple — you get one at the door, hand it to the carver, they write your order, you pay at the exit. Don't lose it. Seriously. Saturday 2pm is smart — 10-15 min wait maybe. And yeah photos are totally fine, go wild.

britt_from_boston: Oh good about photos! One more thing — my mom uses a walker. I heard they have a ramp?

deli_king_nyc: Yeah there's a ramp on Houston Street side, no steps. Inside is open with wide aisles. I've seen folks in wheelchairs there no problem. Bring her!

britt_from_boston: Amazing. Pastrami on rye, fries, half-sour, ticket in the pocket at ALL times. Got it 🫡

results.author: Margot Chen
results.title: Drinking Through History: The Dead Rabbit's Cocktail Menu Is a Masterclass
results.content:
There are cocktail bars that prioritise spectacle — smoke machines, edible glitter, garnishes that look like modern art installations — and then there are cocktail bars that prioritise substance. The Dead Rabbit in Manhattan's Financial District falls decisively into the latter camp, though it manages substance with plenty of style.

The venue occupies a three-storey 1828 building on Water Street, and each floor serves a different purpose. The ground-floor Taproom operates as a traditional Irish pub: dark wood, a working fireplace, sawdust scattered on the floor. It is the sort of place where one could drink a pint of Guinness and eat a respectable Scotch egg without feeling the need to Instagram anything. Upstairs in the Parlor, the cocktail menu is structured as a graphic novel — an ambitious conceit that could feel gimmicky but instead serves as a genuine narrative device. Each chapter corresponds to a period of Irish-American history, and the drinks are researched with what can only be described as obsessive precision. The '1804' cocktail, named for the year of the New York Irish Emancipation, combines Irish whiskey with sherry, yellow Chartreuse, and absinthe. It is balanced, historically plausible, and completely unlike anything else on the market.

A note on accessibility: the building's landmark status means there is no wheelchair access. Three stone steps at the entrance and a narrow staircase to the second floor — the Parlor is genuinely inaccessible to anyone who cannot climb stairs. The venue does welcome dogs in the Taproom, which is a nice concession to the neighbourhood's after-work crowd.

The pricing reflects the venue's pedigree. Cocktails in the Parlor run between $18 and $24, which is standard for a bar of this calibre in New York. The Taproom is more affordable — pints in the $8–10 range, bar snacks around $12–15. Service is polished without being fussy. The bartenders know their product and are happy to talk through the research behind each recipe without delivering a lecture.

The Dead Rabbit has won Best Bar in the World at Tales of the Cocktail multiple times. That sort of accolade can feel dated if a venue rests on its laurels, but the menu here is refreshed seasonally and the historical research continues. It remains a benchmark for what a themed cocktail bar can achieve when the theme is taken seriously rather than treated as decoration.

results.author: FiDi_Guy
results.title: Dead Rabbit still worth the hype in 2025?
results.content:
Thread title: Dead Rabbit still worth the hype in 2025?

FiDi_Guy: Look, I work two blocks away on Water Street so I've been going to the Dead Rabbit for years. Used to be my go-to for after-work pints when it was just a solid Irish bar. Now it's overrun with tourists every single night. Fine by me honestly, keeps the Instagram crowd on the ground floor where they belong.

Anyway, someone asked me last week if it's still worth visiting. The Parlor cocktails are genuinely world-class, I'll give them that. But the Taproom gets packed with suits from the exchange at 5pm and then tourists roll in around 7 and it's a mess. Not a place you'd bring kids obviously — it's 21+ and even if it weren't, the vibe is definitely not family-friendly. Loud after-work crowd, standing room only most nights.

Octavia_NYC: Agree with FiDi_Guy on most of this. I live in Battery Park. The live music on Thursdays in the Taproom is genuinely good — they get proper trad Irish musicians in. That's the best night to go if you ask me. Gets busy but the music cuts through the noise.

FiDi_Guy: Yeah Thursdays are decent actually. The trad sessions are the real deal. I'm just tired of the whole production around the place. But the quality is there. The bartenders upstairs know their stuff, I'll give them that. If you've never been, go on a weeknight and sit at the Parlor bar when it opens at 4, you'll actually get a seat and it's a proper experience.

results.author: Carly Martinez
results.title: A Night at the Dead Rabbit — Yes, It Lives Up to the Hype
results.content:
Okay so my first night in New York and my friend who lives here (well, Brooklyn, which is apparently different) told me I absolutely HAD to go to the Dead Rabbit in the Financial District. And I was like, it's a bar called the Dead Rabbit, isn't that a bit much? But oh my god, guys. It's incredible.

So the building is this gorgeous old 1800s thing on Water Street and you walk in and it's like a cosy Irish pub on the ground floor — dark wood everywhere, a fireplace, the whole thing. But that's just the TAPROOM. If you go up this narrow staircase you get to the Parlor, which is where the serious cocktails happen. The menu is a graphic novel! Each drink is based on a different moment in Irish history in New York. I had one called the '1863' about the Draft Riots, with Irish whiskey and some kind of amaro, and it was honestly one of the best cocktails I've ever had.

Also the dress code thing — I showed up in my travel jeans and a hoodie and they were fine in the Taproom but the host said if I wanted to go upstairs after six I'd need a collared shirt. So I borrowed one from my friend. Smart casual is the vibe up there.

Weird but cool — they let you bring in food from outside? My friend picked up some dumplings from down the street and brought them in and nobody said a thing. We ate dumplings and drank fancy cocktails and I felt like I was getting away with something.

I was traveling solo that first night because my friend was running late, and I sat at the bar in the Taproom. The bartender was super friendly, talked to me about the building's history, recommended a cider I'd never heard of. Really nice vibe for solo drinking, honestly not awkward at all.

Oh and another thing — they don't let you take photos in the Parlor upstairs. The bartender gently told this couple next to me to put their phone away. I kind of get it — everyone's trying to take photos for Instagram and it ruins the mood. But I was low-key sad because the interior up there is SO pretty — velvet seats, dark wallpaper, candlelight. Would have made a great shot. Still, it was nice to just be present and talk instead of staring at my phone.

Anyway, I ended up staying for like three hours which is way longer than I planned. The prices are not cheap — cocktails were like $20ish — but for that quality and the whole experience I think it's worth it. I'd go back in a heartbeat. Next time I'm trying the Irish Coffee, everyone says it's legendary.

results.author: James_Nomad
results.title: Solo at Bemelmans: A Measured Review of the Carlyle's Legendary Bar
results.content:
I went to Bemelmans Bar alone on a Thursday night and here's my honest take.

First impression: the murals are genuinely impressive. I'd seen photos online obviously, and they look nice enough in pictures, but being in the room is different. They wrap around the entire space — walls and ceiling — and the detail is remarkable. Little vignettes of Central Park life: a man walking his dog near the reservoir, children skating at Wollman Rink, horse-drawn carriages. Bemelmans apparently painted them in exchange for free rent at the hotel, which seems like one of the best deals in art history.

Atmosphere: it's dim and intimate. The bar itself is long and the tables are fairly small. I sat at the bar which I'd recommend for a solo visitor — the bartenders are chatty in a professional way and I learned a fair bit about the history of the place without feeling like I was being upsold.

Cocktails: I had two — a Martini (classic, well-executed, very cold) and a Whiskey Sour (good balance, not too sweet). The pours were generous enough but not overly so. I'd say the quality is what you'd expect from a top-tier hotel bar: consistent, well-made, but not groundbreaking.

Crowd: mostly couples and small groups, a few hotel guests. Solo felt fine — the bar is a good spot for it. People were well-dressed, mostly 30s and up. I didn't feel out of place in a blazer and jeans.

Practical notes: no reservation needed for the bar, which is convenient. Service was attentive but not hovering. They don't allow photos, which the staff enforce politely. I actually appreciated it — everyone was present rather than on their phones.

Would I go back? Probably, if someone else was paying. One visit is probably enough unless you're a hotel guest or a serious cocktail enthusiast. I spent about 90 minutes there, had two drinks, and left satisfied. The pianist was good — Sinatra standards, nothing too flashy.

Overall: a solid 4/5 for atmosphere and history, 3.Worth doing once.

results.author: MumOnTheMove_NYC
results.title: One World Observatory with Kids: What You Need to Know Before You Go
results.content:
Taking kids to an observation deck can go one of two ways — either they're glued to the windows pointing at everything or they're bored within ten minutes asking for snacks. At One World Observatory, I'm happy to report it was definitely the first option.

First things first: book your tickets online before you go. They don't sell walk-up tickets at all, everything's timed entry. We booked the 10am slot which worked well — the queues weren't bad and the kids were still fresh. If you go later in the day expect bigger crowds.

The elevator ride alone is a huge hit with little ones. The ceiling shows a time-lapse of New York's skyline changing as you go up, and my six-year-old was mesmerised. It takes about 47 seconds to reach the 102nd floor and my ears did pop a bit — my youngest (four) said her ears felt funny but she was fine after a few seconds.

Once you're up there, the windows are floor-to-ceiling and even small children can see out easily. My four-year-old could see the Statue of Liberty without me having to lift her up, which was a relief for my arms. There are interactive touchscreens by the windows where you can point at landmarks and it tells you what they are — my six-year-old loved playing with those and it kept her engaged for ages.

There's a cafe on-site for snacks and drinks if you need a break, which definitely came in handy. The See Forever Theater at the start is a short film about New York's history and it's fine for kids aged five and up — the music swells and it's quite dramatic. My four-year-old got a bit fidgety but it's only about a minute long so manageable.

We spent about an hour and a half up there which felt about right. The gift shop at the end had some reasonably priced souvenirs which the kids loved. All in all a great family outing.

results.author: solo_journey
results.title: Solo at the Top: My Afternoon at One World Observatory
results.content:
Had a rough couple of weeks at work and booked a solo trip to New York on impulse. I needed somewhere quiet to just sit and think, which is how I ended up at One World Observatory on a Tuesday afternoon.

I went in with pretty low expectations — observation decks always feel like you're paying to be herded through a turnstile. And yeah, the security line was a thing, but it moved fast enough. The staff were friendly and efficient.

The See Forever Theater was a nice surprise. A quick film about New York's history with a sweeping soundtrack — I actually got a bit emotional standing there in the dark. It hits different when you're alone and already feeling a bit raw.

The elevator is genuinely impressive. The ceiling projection showing the skyline evolving as you rise... I don't know, it got me. There's something about going up that fast in a glass capsule with strangers that makes you feel both anonymous and connected. Probably overthinking it but that's what solo travel does to you.

Upstairs, I just found a spot by the south-facing windows and stood there for maybe 45 minutes watching the boats in the harbor. The light was soft and grey, December clouds hanging low. The city below looked manageable from up there — all the noise and stress reduced to tiny dots moving between buildings. It felt like the right place to be that day.

The interactive touchscreens are fun to play with. I spent a while identifying landmarks and learning facts about the Financial District buildings below. The See Forever virtual display showing what the area looked like centuries ago was fascinating.

Stayed for about two hours. Grabbed a coffee from the cafe before heading down. Not cheap at $44 but for the headspace it gave me? Worth it.

results.author: Elena Marchetti
results.title: One World Observatory: 1,776 Feet Above Lower Manhattan
results.content:
The golden hour light at One World Observatory is something I'll be chasing for a long time. I showed up about an hour before sunset on a clear November weekday — the kind of day where the air is crisp and the sky does that slow burn from pale blue to lavender to amber.

What really struck me wasn't just the height — though 102 floors is undeniably impressive — it was how the glass wraps all the way around. You can shoot in nearly every direction without obstruction. The skyline spreads out like a living map: the Statue of Liberty looking small and delicate in the harbor, the Brooklyn Bridge tracing its elegant arc across the East River, the Empire State Building and Chrysler Building standing tall to the north.

For composition, I'd recommend the south-facing windows around sunset. The light rakes across the Financial District buildings below, and the harbor turns into a sheet of gold. The SkyPod elevator ride is worth filming too — the ceiling projection shows a time-lapse of New York's skyline evolving, which is a clever touch.

I was worried about reflections in the glass, but honestly? The glare management is excellent. At certain angles you barely notice the glass at all. Bring a polarizer if you're serious about eliminating reflections, but you can get clean shots without one.

The interactive touchscreens by the windows are handy for identifying landmarks — useful when you're trying to frame a specific building and need to know exactly where it sits.

One thing: the lighting inside the observatory shifts throughout the day to match the conditions outside, which creates a really natural atmosphere for photography. No harsh overhead fluorescents ruining the mood. The space stays relatively calm even when it's busy — people are mostly quiet, just staring out at the city.

All the major observatories in New York have their strengths, but for the quality of daylight and the unobstructed panoramic field of view, One World Observatory is my pick for serious photography.

results.author: Anika Patel
results.title: Golden hour from the Top of the Rock — a photographer's perspective
results.content:
There's a particular moment at Top of the Rock about forty minutes before sunset when the light turns this deep, honeyed gold that wraps itself around every building in Manhattan. I've shot skyline panoramas from a dozen different perches across this city — the Empire State, One World Trade, even a helicopter over the Hudson — but nothing captures the geometry of New York quite like the vantage point from 30 Rock.

Looking south you get the Empire State Building rising dead centre of the frame, with the Flatiron and Hudson Yards catching that last warm light on their glass facades. You can frame the Chrysler spire against the soft blue of the East River beyond — a silhouette shot I've been chasing for years. The art deco metalwork of the railings creates this beautiful foreground texture against the soft cityscape behind.

I arrived around 3.30pm on a Tuesday in October and had about ninety minutes of gorgeous shooting before golden hour. The west-facing side is where you want to be for sunset — the light falls across Central Park in long amber strips and the building shadows stretch out like sundials. Tripods aren't allowed on the deck which is a pain, but the handrails are wide enough to rest a lens on if you're careful. I got fantastic handheld shots at 1/30th by bracing against the railing.

What surprised me was how the terrace is designed — the wrap-around outdoor deck means you're never fighting for a single viewpoint. Even with sixty or seventy people up there, I always found a spot. The glass panels on the lower railing are angled so you can shoot clean frames without reflections if you get your lens right up against the glass. Someone clearly thought about photographers.

As the sun dipped below the horizon the city started winking on — first the Empire State lit up in its nightly colours, then the towers of Midtown, then the distant bridges. By 6pm the whole skyline was an electric tapestry of light. The temperature dropped fast but I couldn't pull myself away. I shot about four hundred frames. Maybe half are keepers.

For any photographer visiting New York — put Top of the Rock on your list. Go on a clear weekday, aim for ninety minutes before sunset, bring a lens that handles low light. The golden hour here is something else.

results.author: MumOnTheMove
results.title: Statue of Liberty with kids: a survival guide
results.content:
Taking kids to the Statue of Liberty. Sounds daunting, right? I've done it three times now with children ranging from 4 to 11, so here's the field-tested version.

First: book the earliest ferry slot you can find. The 8:30 from Battery Park. If you're on the 10:30 or later, you're queueing with every school trip in the tristate area. Our 8:30 run? We walked straight onto the boat. Coming back at noon? The queue snaked halfway across the island. So book tickets weeks in advance, not days. The crown tickets sell out months ahead — we did pedestal access and that was plenty.

Second: pack snacks. There's a cafe on Liberty Island but the prices made me wince and the line was twenty minutes. They won't let you bring a full cooler — I tried a small soft-sided lunch bag with sandwiches and fruit and nobody batted an eye. Just leave the giant picnic kit at home.

Third: stroller logistics. The ferry is stroller-friendly, crew helped us board no problem. On Liberty Island the paths are paved and smooth — you can push a stroller all the way around. The pedestal elevator is big enough for a double stroller, which surprised me. So if you're worried about accessibility with little ones, don't be. It's all step-free and easy to navigate.

Fourth: keep it short. Two hours on the island is about max for kids under 8. Walk the perimeter, see the statue up close, visit the museum in the pedestal (the kids loved the old photos of immigrants), then get back on the ferry. Don't try to do Ellis Island on the same ticket unless your kids are older — that's a whole second island and they'll be done by then.

Fifth: bathrooms. There's a clean restroom near the ferry dock on Liberty Island. Use it before you queue for the return boat. That's the pro tip right there.

results.author: Jake Morrison
results.title: My First Time at MoMA — I Had No Idea What I Was Getting Into
results.content:
Okay so I finally made it to MoMA on my last day in New York and oh my god, I had no idea it was THAT big. Like, I knew it was a famous museum obviously, but the scale of it just hits you when you walk into that huge white atrium with the giant escalators going up and up and up.

First thing — you HAVE to book tickets online in advance. I almost didn't and my hotel concierge warned me, thank god, because the line for walk-ups was like down the block. I booked for 10:30 AM slot and it was perfect — straight in, no waiting. Do that. Seriously.

Getting there was interesting. I took the subway to 5th Ave/53rd Street and walked maybe two minutes. Honestly driving in Midtown seems like a nightmare and I saw zero parking anywhere nearby, so don't even think about renting a car for this one. Subway or walk, that's the move.

I spent the first hour completely lost in the modern wing — there's just so much. Saw the Van Gogh Starry Night which obviously is the headliner and there's always a crowd around it, but honestly the stuff I loved most were things I'd never heard of. There's this huge Monet water lilies installation that takes up an entire curved room and I sat there for like fifteen minutes just staring. And the Pollock drip paintings? I always thought they looked kinda random in photos but in person you can see the physicality of it, like you can tell how his arm moved.

The building itself is gorgeous too — all glass and white marble and clean lines. I took about a million photos, especially in the sculpture garden on the ground floor which is this peaceful outdoor space right in the middle of everything. Had lunch at Cafe 2 which was decent for museum food, not cheap but not outrageous either.

Oh and I almost forgot — the Peggy Guggenheim collection room! That was a surprise highlight. I didn't know MoMA had so much surrealist stuff. Three hours went by like nothing.
